This post shows operations and applications over matrix, refers to Wikipedia.

The transpose of a matrix A, denoted by A^T is the matrix obtained by swapping the rows and columns of A. It satisfies the following properties:
(A^T)^T = A
(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T
(cA)^T = cA^T
(AB)^T = B^TA^T

If the following condition satisfies:
a_{ij} = a_{ji} \quad \forall i,j
Then the matrix is called symmetric.

A square matrix A is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:
A = A^T
This also implies A^{-1} A^T = I

The determinant of a n\times n square matrix A is commonly denoted \det A or |A|. It satisfies the following properties:
\det A^T = \det A
\det AB = \det A \det B
\det \lambda A = \lambda ^n \det A
To compute the inverse of a matrix, we need Adjugate matrix.

If A is a square matrix, then the minor of the entry in the i-th row and j-th column (also called the (i, j) minor, or a first minor) is the determinant of the sub-matrix formed by deleting the i-th row and j-th column. The (i, j) minor is denoted as M_{ij}. The Cofactor is obtained by multiplying the minor by (-1)^{i+j}.

The matrix formed by all of the cofactors of a square matrix A is called the cofactor matrix, or comatrix:
C = \left [ \begin {array}{cccc} C_{11} & C_{12} & \cdots & C_{1n} \\ C_{21} & C_{22} & \cdots & C_{2n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ C_{n1} & C_{n2} & \cdots & C_{nn} \end {array} \right ]
The Adjugate matrix of A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

Then the inverse of A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix times the reciprocal of the determinant of A:
A^{-1} = \frac {1}{\det A} \cdot \text {adj} A = \frac {1}{\det A} \cdot C^T
A square matrix that is not invertible is called singular or degenerate

html:p.fr:tex: A \cdot \text {adj} A = \text {adj} A \cdot A = \det A \cdot I

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let A \cdot \text {adj} A = (b_{ij}) and we have
b_{ij} = a_{i1}A_{j1} + a_{i2}A_{j2} + \cdots + a_{in}A_{jn} = \delta _{ij} \cdot \det A
Hence we have A \cdot \text {adj} A = \det A \cdot I

A matrix polynomial is a polynomial with square matrices as variables. The general form of a matrix polynomial is:
P(A) = \sum _{i=0}^{n} a_i A^i
where A^0 = I is the identity matrix.

If A is a diagonal matrix, then the polynomial of A is the diagonal matrix of the polynomial of the diagonal elements of A.
p(A) = \begin {bmatrix} p(a_{11}) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & p(a_{22}) & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & p(a_{nn}) \end {bmatrix}

If A = P\Lambda P^{-1}, then A^k = P \Lambda ^k P^{-1} and hence
p(A) = a_0 I + a_1 A + a_2 A^2 + \cdots + a_n A^n = P \Lambda P^{-1}

Consider a system of n linear equations for n unknowns, represented in matrix multiplication form as follows:
A \cdot X = B
where A is a square matrix of order n, X is a column matrix of order n and B is a column matrix of order n.
X = \begin {bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end {bmatrix}
The Cramer's rule states that the solution to the system of equations is given by:
x_i = \frac {\text {det}(A_i)}{\text {det}(A)}
where A_i is the matrix obtained by replacing the ith column of A by B.
Matrix partitioning is the process of dividing a matrix into smaller submatrices. This is often done to simplify the computation of matrix operations, such as matrix multiplication.

There are three types of elementary matrices, which correspond to three types of row operations (respectively, column operations, row operations are equivalent to multiplying on the left by the corresponding elementary matrix, and column operations are equivalent to multiplying on the right by the corresponding elementary matrix):
Row switching: A row within the matrix can be switched with another row.
P_{i,j} = \begin {bmatrix} 1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & 0 & & 1 \\ & & & \ddots \\ & & 1 & & 0 \\ & & & & & \ddots \\ & & & & & & 1 \end {bmatrix}
Row multiplication: Each element in a row can be multiplied by a non-zero constant.
D_i(k) = \text {diag} (1, \cdots , k, \cdots , 1)
Row additio: A row can be replaced by the sum of that row and a multiple of another row.
T_{i,j} = \begin {bmatrix} 1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & 1 & & k \\ & & & \ddots \\ & & & & 1 \\ & & & & & \ddots \\ & & & & & & 1 \end {bmatrix}

Two matrices A,B are column / row equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of elementary operations, denoted A \sim B. The column / row equivalence is an equivalence relation.

We can show that a matrix A is invertible iff there are finite elementary matrices E_1, E_2, \cdots , E_n such that
A = E_1E_2\cdots E_n

From above we can deduce that a square matrix A is invertible iff A\sim E. This trick can be used for solving a linear system and computing the inverse of a matrix. For instance, given AX=B we can solve X by the following steps: Let P be a matrix such that PA=I where I is the identity matrix. Hence P = A^{-1} and we have X = PB, we can do elementary operations over matrix (A, B) to get the solution of X.
Now let's talk about the concept of rank. In linear algebra, the (column)rank of a matrix A is the dimension of the vector space generated (or spanned) by its columns.

The rank of a linear map or operator \Phi is defined as the dimension of its range:
\text {rank}(M)\equiv \dim (\text {range }(M))
Note that the range (column space) of a matrix M is the span of its column vectors.

Similarly we can define the row rank of a matrix. A fundamental result in linear algebra is that the column rank and the row rank are always equal. Hence we can simply call it the rank of a matrix. If the column rank equals to the column size, we say that the matrix is full column rank.

A common approach to finding the rank of a matrix is to reduce it to a simpler form, generally row echelon form, by elementary row operations. Row operations do not change the row space (hence do not change the row rank), and, being invertible, map the column space to an isomorphic space (hence do not change the column rank).
A \sim B \implies \text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(B) \\ \text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(A^T)
Once in row echelon form, the rank is clearly the same for both row rank and column rank, and equals to the number of pivots (or basic columns) and also the number of non-zero rows.

A matrix is in row echelon form if
All rows having only zero entries are at the bottom
The leading entry (that is, the left-most nonzero entry) of every nonzero row, called the pivot, is on the right of the leading entry of every row above.
Some texts add the condition that the leading coefficient must be 1 while others require this only in reduced row echelon form.

The determinantal rank of a matrix is the order of the largest non-zero minor of the matrix. It is also the number of non-zero eigenvalues of the matrix. This does not give an efficient way of computing the rank, but it is useful theoretically: a single non-zero minor witnesses a lower bound for the rank of the matrix, which can be useful to prove that certain operations do not lower the rank of a matrix.

We can conclude the properties of rank:
\begin {align*} &0 \leq \text {rank}(A_{m\times n}) \leq \min (m,n) \\ &\text {rank}(A^T) = \text {rank}(A) \\ & A \sim B \implies \text {rank}(A)=\text {rank}(B) \\ & P, Q \text { is invertible} \implies \text {rank}(PAQ) = \text {rank}(A) \\ & \max (\text {rank}(A), \text {rank}(B)) \leq \text {rank}(A, B) \leq \text {rank}(A) + \text {rank}(B) \\ & \text {rank}(A+B) \leq \text {rank}(A) + \text {rank}(B) \\ & \text {rank}(AB) \leq \min (\text {rank}(A), \text {rank}(B)) \\ & A_{m\times n}B_{n\times l} = O\implies \text {rank}(A) + \text {rank}(B) \leq n \end {align*}

With such properties we can prove an important theorem:
AB = O \land A \text { is full rank} \implies B = O
which is known as the cancellation law of matrix multiplication.

The rank of a matrix is also related to the solution of a linear system. If the rank of the coefficient matrix is less than the rank of the augmented matrix, then the system is inconsistent. Hence there does not exist a solution. Similarly we have the following discussion: For a n-variable linear system Ax = b
If \text {rank}(A) < \text {rank}(A,b), the solution does not exist.
If \text {rank}(A)=\text {rank}(A,b)=n, there is a unique solution.
If \text {rank}(A)=\text {rank}(A,b)<n, there are infinite solutions.
This leads two fundamental theorems of linear systems:
n-variable regular linear system Ax = 0 has a non-trivial solution iff \text {rank}(A) < n.
Matrix equation AX = B has solutions iff \text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(A,B).

Let V be a vector space over a field F. Let v_1, \dots , v_n be vectors in V. A linear combination of v_1, \dots , v_n is an expression of the form
a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n
where a_1, \dots , a_n \in F.

Given two sets of vectors, we say that they are equal iff their elements can write as linear combinations of each other. This condition can be written using rank:
\text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(B) = \text {rank}(A, B)

A set of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is called linearly independent if a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n = 0 implies that a_1 = \dots = a_n = 0. The trivial case of \{0\} is also considered linearly independent.

Any square matrix A can be written as the sum of a symmetric and antisymmetric matrix:
A = A_S + A_A
where A_S is the symmetric part and A_A is the antisymmetric part.
A_S = \frac {1}{2}(A + A^T)
where A_S is a symmetric matrix
A_A = \frac {1}{2}(A - A^T)
where A_A is an antisymmetric matrix
